name: Robert Morris
category: Computer scientist / internet worm author / YC partner
milestone_by_age_26: Released the Morris worm from MIT on November 2, 1988 while a Cornell first-year graduate student at age 22—the first widely disruptive internet worm—and became the first person convicted under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.
early_history_summary: Born November 8, 1965 to Bell Labs Unix/Multics cryptographer Robert Morris Sr. and Anne Farlow Morris; raised in New Jersey and educated at The Peck School and Delbarton. Harvard BA then Cornell CS graduate school; prior password-cracking and systems interest from high school and early university years.
family_context_summary: Father Robert Morris was a Bell Labs computer scientist who helped design Multics and Unix and later became chief scientist at the NSA National Computer Security Center; mother Anne Farlow Morris.
parent_family_domain_summary: Direct parental domain expertise in Unix, Multics, and computer security—rare scarce-skill transfer in 1970s–80s systems software.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bell Labs Unix father, Harvard/Cornell, early internet security wave, password/systems depth
evidence_summary: Morris's ≤26 milestone is the 1988 Morris worm at age 22—first major internet worm and first CFAA conviction—built on deep systems skill cultivated with a Unix/security father and elite CS training. Later co-founded Viaweb (sold to Yahoo) and Y Combinator and became MIT tenured professor; family-domain and institutional pipeline advantages are strongly documented.
starting_point: Born 1965 in the US to Bell Labs Unix cryptographer Robert Morris Sr.; raised Millington NJ with elite prep schooling before Harvard and Cornell CS.
current_position: MIT EECS professor (tenure 2006); Y Combinator partner; National Academy of Engineering member (2019); lives and works in the US academic/startup ecosystem.

trajectory.event: Released the Morris worm from MIT; first widely disruptive internet worm and first CFAA prosecution.
Sentenced after conviction under CFAA (probation, community service, fine).
Co-founded Viaweb with Paul Graham; sold to Yahoo (Yahoo Store) for ~$49M in 1998.
Received Harvard PhD in Applied Sciences; joined MIT as assistant professor.
Co-founded Y Combinator with Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, and Trevor Blackwell.
Awarded tenure at MIT.
Elected to the National Academy of Engineering.

name: Richard Liu
milestone_by_age_26: Founded Jingdong (JD Multimedia) as a Zhongguancun magneto-optical retail store in June 1998 at age 25, the seed of what became JD.com, one of China's largest e-commerce platforms.
early_history_summary: Born March 10, 1973 in Suqian, Jiangsu to a poor rural family. Renmin University sociology/law graduate (1996); failed restaurant venture as a student left him deep in debt; worked at Japan Life before founding Jingdong in Beijing's electronics market, later pivoting online after SARS (2003–04).
family_context_summary: Grew up in poverty in rural Suqian, Jiangsu; family loans funded an early failed restaurant; later returned home for village philanthropy.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a retail/tech family pipeline in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Zhongguancun retail, poverty catalyst, China e-commerce wave, SARS pivot online
evidence_summary: Liu's ≤26 milestone is founding Jingdong retail in June 1998 at 25 in Beijing's Zhongguancun, later scaled into JD.com (Nasdaq IPO 2014). Poverty adversity, direct retail ops immersion, and China internet commerce wave dominate the advantage stack; inherited capital/networks are not documented.
starting_point: Born 1973 in rural Suqian, Jiangsu into poverty; Renmin University sociology graduate who failed an early restaurant before Beijing retail entrepreneurship.
current_position: Chairman of JD.com (stepped down as CEO 2022); multi-billionaire Chinese e-commerce founder; philanthropist (major share pledges to charity).

trajectory.event: Founded Jingdong magneto-optical retail store in Zhongguancun, Beijing.
Launched online retail after SARS forced brick-and-mortar rethink; closed offline stores by 2005.
Expanded JD beyond electronics into full-category e-commerce.
JD.com IPO on Nasdaq raised ~$1.8B, then largest Chinese internet IPO in New York.
Stepped down as CEO to chairman role; later pledged large JD share blocks to charity.

name: Elad Gil
milestone_by_age_26: No material independently verifiable founder/operator breakout by age 26 (~2002). Mixer Labs co-founded ~2007 (age ~30–31) and sold to Twitter; Color Genomics founded 2013 (age ~37). MIT biology PhD and early Google mobile/AdSense work are career prep after 26, not a dated ≤26 breakout milestone.
family_context_summary: Born in Israel; immigrated to the US in youth; detailed parental occupations not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Defining founder milestones (Mixer Labs ~2007, Color 2013) and high-profile angel investing arrived well after age 26. No specific dated material founding/research breakout by 26 found in reviewed sources.

name: Derek Sivers
milestone_by_age_26: No material independently verifiable founder breakout by age 26 (1995). CD Baby was started ~1997–1998 at about age 28–29 (he has described starting the company at 29). Earlier professional musician/circus work is not treated as the career-defining tech/commerce milestone.
family_context_summary: Born 1969 Berkeley, California; raised partly Chicago; detailed parental occupations not central in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a music-tech family pipeline in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: CD Baby founding (~1998) at ~28–29 is the defining milestone and falls after age 26. No earlier dated material founder/engineer breakout found.

name: Patrick McKenzie
milestone_by_age_26: Launched Bingo Card Creator in 2006 at about age 22—an early successful single-founder desktop/SaaS product for teachers that later funded full-time entrepreneurship and the influential patio11 blog/HN persona.
early_history_summary: American software founder best known online as patio11; started Bingo Card Creator while working as a salaryman-style software engineer in Japan, iterated on pricing and marketing publicly, and built one of the best-documented indie bootstrap case studies of the late 2000s.
family_context_summary: Not richly documented in reviewed sources; later associated with Chicago; early career included software employment in Japan.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Hacker News distribution, indie SaaS wave, public marketing experiments, Bingo Card Creator
evidence_summary: McKenzie's ≤26 milestone is Bingo Card Creator (2006, age ~22), a real revenue business that seeded the patio11 brand. Primary advantages are product insight plus online community distribution (HN/blogs) rather than family capital or elite pipelines; family background is under-documented.
starting_point: Born ~1984; early career software engineer who built Bingo Card Creator as a side business while working in Japan.
current_position: Well-known indie founder/advisor and internet business writer (patio11); previously Stripe (including Atlas-related work); based in Chicago area.

trajectory.event: Launched Bingo Card Creator, beginning multi-year indie SaaS business.
Quit day job after BCC and consulting income covered living costs.
Sold Bingo Card Creator after ~9 years of operation.
Joined Stripe; became a prominent public voice on payments and startups.

name: Perry Chen
milestone_by_age_26: No material independently verifiable breakout by age 26 (2002). Crowdfunding idea originated ~2001–02 but Kickstarter only launched publicly April 28, 2009 at about age 32–33 with cofounders Yancey Strickler and Charles Adler. Having an idea alone is not coded as a material milestone.
family_context_summary: Not richly documented in reviewed sources for early family platform.
evidence_summary: Kickstarter public launch 2009 (~age 33) is the defining milestone; earlier concept notes are not material shipped products or companies. No ≤26 dated breakout found.

name: Yancey Strickler
milestone_by_age_26: No material independently verifiable cofounder breakout by age 26 (Nov 2004). Joined Kickstarter effort ~2005 (age ~26–27) and publicly launched April 2009 at age 30. Prior music journalism is not treated as the defining founder milestone.
family_context_summary: Raised on a farm in Clover Hollow, Virginia; William & Mary graduate; early career music critic.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a tech/startup family pipeline.
evidence_summary: Kickstarter launch 2009 at age 30 is defining; collaboration beginning ~2005 is at/after the age-26 boundary without a shipped platform. Marked ineligible.

name: Charles Adler
milestone_by_age_26: No material independently verifiable breakout by age 26 (2002). Joined Perry Chen and Yancey Strickler on Kickstarter around 2006 as design cofounder; platform launched 2009 at about age 32–33.
family_context_summary: Not richly documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Kickstarter design cofounding and 2009 launch occurred in early 30s. No ≤26 material milestone found.

name: Alex Finn
milestone_by_age_26: No material independently verifiable breakout by age 26 (2021) found in reviewed sources. Public traction centers on Creator Buddy / AI content products launched ~2024–2025 (age ~29–30) and later creator-economy AI education; earlier dated founder milestones ≤26 were not verified with two sources.
evidence_summary: Visible breakout product Creator Buddy and related AI creator business arrived after age 26. Conservative ineligibility given sparse dated early milestones.

name: Dan Shipper
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Fire and Ice (//FIRE//) around 2009–2010 at about age 19–20, an early social/discovery product that drew TechCrunch attention and led to Harvard Business Review recognition as a young entrepreneur by age ~20.
early_history_summary: Serial product founder who started Fire and Ice while young, later co-founded other products (including paths into Divinations/Every with Nathan Baschez), and built a writing-first AI media company. Early public profile as teen/early-20s founder is documented in tech press.
family_context_summary: Not richly documented in reviewed English sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: teen founding, Fire and Ice, later Every/AI writing, cofounder networks
evidence_summary: Shipper's ≤26 milestone is early company founding (Fire and Ice ~19–20) with public tech-press validation. Later Every/AI media success compounds writing and product skill; family advantages are not documented.
starting_point: Born ~1990; early product founder who launched Fire and Ice as a teenager/early-20s entrepreneur.
current_position: Cofounder/CEO of Every, an AI-era writing and software media company; active essayist on AI and work.

trajectory.event: Fire and Ice / early startup work drew TechCrunch coverage; recognized among young entrepreneurs.
With Nathan Baschez launched Divinations newsletter, seed of Every.
Built Every into a paid writing/software business around AI-augmented knowledge work.
Every became a prominent AI-native media and product company under Shipper's leadership.

name: Nathan Baschez
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Product Hunt with Ryan Hoover in November 2013 at about age 25, building one of the defining early distribution platforms for startups and makers.
early_history_summary: Product-minded writer/operator who helped start Product Hunt in 2013, later worked on growth products, and co-created Divinations/Every with Dan Shipper as a writing-first company. Early career combined content and product execution in Silicon Valley maker communities.
family_context_summary: Not richly documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Product Hunt, Ryan Hoover cofounder, SF maker community, later Every/Divinations
evidence_summary: Baschez's ≤26 milestone is co-founding Product Hunt (2013, age ~25) with Ryan Hoover—a major distribution platform for startups. Peer cofounder chemistry, Bay Area maker networks, and platform-native distribution are the clearest advantages.
starting_point: Born ~1988; Silicon Valley product/writing operator who co-founded Product Hunt in his mid-20s.
current_position: Cofounder associated with Every / Divinations writing and product work; continues as a product-minded writer and operator.

trajectory.event: Co-founded Product Hunt with Ryan Hoover.
Product Hunt acquired by AngelList, validating the platform's role in startup discovery.
Launched Divinations newsletter with Dan Shipper, precursor to Every.
Scaled Every as a paid writing and software business.

name: Linus Sebastian
milestone_by_age_26: Created the Linus Tech Tips YouTube channel on November 24, 2008 at age 22 while producing tech content for NCIX, establishing the brand that later became Linus Media Group and one of the largest tech YouTube networks.
early_history_summary: Canadian tech communicator who started as an NCIX retail/demo employee making product videos, spun out Linus Tech Tips as a personal channel in 2008, and formalized Linus Media Group in 2013 after leaving NCIX. Built a multi-channel tech media company from early YouTube adoption.
family_context_summary: Born in British Columbia, Canada; early work at NCIX computer retailer provided domain immersion; detailed parental occupations not central in sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as a media/tech family pipeline in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: YouTube tech wave, NCIX retail domain, Linus Tech Tips brand, later LMG scale
evidence_summary: Sebastian's ≤26 milestone is founding Linus Tech Tips (2008, age 22) from NCIX content work—platform-native distribution plus PC-retail domain exposure. LMG formalization in 2013 (age 27) is later scale-up of that early channel asset.
starting_point: Born 1986 in British Columbia; entered tech retail/content via NCIX before spinning out Linus Tech Tips.
current_position: Founder/face of Linus Media Group (Linus Tech Tips and sister channels); major tech YouTube operator based in Canada.

trajectory.event: Created Linus Tech Tips YouTube channel while producing NCIX tech videos.
Left NCIX and founded Linus Media Group as an independent media company.
Scaled multi-channel tech network and warehouse/studio production model.
Continued as one of the largest tech YouTube operators amid industry scrutiny and transparency debates.
